messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 49

Elias sits across from me, his hands resting on a worn leather briefcase that hasn’t opened in weeks. At sixty-three, his posture carries the weight of decades spent chasing stories across the continent, but lately, the weight has settled differently. It lives in his shoulders, in the way his eyes track the door every time someone enters the building. We have been meeting for months, and the narrative of his past and present slowly unfolds in the quiet spaces between his sentences. It began six years ago, on a Tuesday that started like any other. He was at his desk in Nairobi, editing a feature on urban development, when his phone vibrated with a number he knew by heart. His younger brother, Kwame, had been caught in a sudden outbreak of violence during a student rally in Kampala. The line crackled with static and a voice that did not belong to a paramedic. Elias booked the next flight, told his wife, Amara, to wait at the airport, and flew into a city he had only known through news wires. He stood in a sterile hospital room while they pulled a sheet over Kwame’s face. He signed papers. He returned home. The story was printed. The world moved on. For a while, he tried to outrun the silence that followed. He took on deeper assignments, chasing conflict zones and corporate scandals with restless precision. His byline grew longer, but his sleep grew shorter. Now, his apartment feels more like a perimeter than a home. He checks the deadbolt three times before bed. He avoids highways and turns off the radio when emergency sirens bleed through the windows. When he tries to write, the keyboard feels like a mirror. The words won’t come unless he’s chasing something else, but lately, even the chase drains him. He sits for hours, cursor blinking, staring at a half-finished draft until the light fades. He tells himself it’s just writer’s block, but we both know it is not. Amara notices the distance, though she does not name it. They share a bed, but she often wakes to find him standing by the window, watching the street below. His hands are steady now, but his breathing is shallow. He laughs at dinner parties when the conversation turns to family, but the laugh stops short, caught behind his ribs. He still calls his sister-in-law every Sunday, but he has stopped asking about her children’s birthdays. He keeps a box of Kwame’s notebooks in the back of his closet, wrapped in plastic, untouched. When the power goes out, he lights a single candle and reads through them until his eyes burn. Journalism used to be his rhythm. Now it is a metronome he has to wind every morning. He attends editorial meetings but speaks less, his pen tapping a quiet rhythm against his notepad. He used to lean into the chaos of a developing story, but now it feels like a trap. He leaves early, claiming deadlines, but walks a longer route home, passing the hospital twice. He tells himself he is just being careful. He tells himself the past is a closed case file. As an African man who spent his career translating other people’s crises into print, he now finds himself trapped in the static of his own. Some nights, when the house is quiet and the city hums beyond the glass, he sits on the edge of the bed and watches his wife sleep. He reaches for her hand, then pulls back. He does not know how to bridge the space between the man who left six years ago and the man who returns each evening. He only knows that the news never stops breaking, and he is still waiting for a headline that will make it stop.
